description.narrative:
The programme aligns to the Global Strategic Framework as follows:
 Just Economies
a. Economic models prevent exploitation and unsustainable extraction. b. Tax systems are fair within and across nations. c. Trade and food systems are fair and sustainable.
Climate Justice a. Greenhouse gas emissions are reduced to limit global heating by 1.5 degrees Celsius. b. Local expertise and women’s leadership is resourced to build resilience and shape solutions. c. Climate finance is adequate, predictable, and accessible forthe poor and vulnerable communities.
 Accountable Governance a. Robust governance frameworks provide safe spaces for people to hold duty bearers to account. b. Feminist and youth movements are adequately supported andresourced. c. Effective digital rights mechanisms regulate government and corporate actors.
Change Goals:
1. Inclusive, equitable and sustainable growth and development models that dignify and improve the lives of vulnerable and marginalized groups – i.e. women, youth, PWD and minority groups. 2. Agriculture and food systems that are resilient, inclusive and climate-smart, and which guarantees that small-scale food producers earn a decent living and can build better lives for themselves.
Strategic Objective 3.4.1: Economic models prevent exploitation and unsustainable extraction.
3.4.1.1 Transparent and robust systems for sustainable natural resource extraction
 20 civil society organisations’ capacity strengthened to monitor EITI implementation of the 2023 EITI Standards in Zambia and Mozambique.  3 Campaigns anchored on the Publish What You Pay (PWYP) ‘Disclose the Deal Campaign’ in Zambia, Mozambique, and Zimbabwe for E.I value chain transparency.  Develop and publish 4 policy briefs to stimulate public participation and accountable governance in resource rich countries.  Increase by 10% the number of tax administration authorities’ staff in Zambia, Mozambique, and Zimbabwe capacity in mineral fiscal governance through learning platforms.  Produce and disseminate one research and advocacy case study on extractive industries fiscal or socio-environmental model.  200 CSOs and mining communities supported to dialogue on mining and taxation laws/policies development and implementation through symposiums and national mining indabas in Zambia and Zimbabwe.  Co-convene two regional multi-stakeholder platforms on transparent and robust systems in minerals resources extraction which include the Alternative Mining Indaba (AMI) and SADC People Summit  5000 people reached by Zambia and Mozambique Advocacy Campaigns on subnational revenue sharing mechanisms from extractive industries in Mozambique and Zambia for gender sensitive service delivery and humanitarian action.
3.4.1.2. Increased financial transparency and pro-poor accountability for EI revenue generation and expenditure.
 Increase by 20% number of mining, oil and gas contracts disclosed by governments in Zambia, Mozambique, and Zimbabwe  Increase by 25% number of women’s Rightsand Extractive Industries civil society organisations participating in mineral revenue accountability platforms at national and sub-national level for improved service delivery.  Co-convene with Tax Justice Network-Africa the Pan African Conference on Taxationand Illicit Financial Flows and meetings for optimum revenue generation and management of the EI sector.  2 EITI reports analysed by civil society in the Zambia and Mozambique on the national reports to validate EI revenue generation and expenditure.  Increase by 30% number of public understanding EI taxation and revenue collection and expenditure laws and rules in Zambia, Zimbabwe and Mozambique
3.4.1.3. Adoption and implementation of laws and policies respecting FPIC
 Increased number of laws and regulations on FPIC and human rights due diligence in mining operations  Increase by 20% technical support to human rights defenders advocating for human rights protection and FPIC in the extractive sector.  Produce and disseminate 3 media stories using different platforms raising awareness around FPIC, conflict and community rights violations in relation to extractive industries in Mozambique, Zambia and Zimbabwe.
Strategic Objective 3.4.2: Improved Fiscal justice for countries in SAF
3.4.2.1 Public finance management systems are gender just, robust, and transparent.
 Organise one SAF Inequality Conference that brings together all the three thematic pillars and partners  Promote and support citizens participation in the national planning and budgeting processes in Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Malawi.  Undertake analyses of public finance management and national planning and budgeting policies in Zambia, Malawi, Zimbabwe and Mozambique to establish gaps, challenges and opportunities for citizens participation in public finance management and national planning and budgeting.  Build capacity of government officials, members of parliament, CSOs and citizens in gender responsive budgeting.  In collaboration with the GJ team support Partners advocacy work on gender responsive government budgeting  Develop position papers on challenges and recommendations on robust, transparent and inclusive public finance management systems and practices in Zambia,Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Malawi  Undertake review and alignment of country Public Finance Management Act with SADC Model Law on Public Finance Management  Sensitization and advocacy towards domestication of SADC model law on Public Finance Management  Conduct country-specific independent research reports (Malawi and Zambia) on debt sustainability and promote a series of country-specific workshops on debt sustainability and debt restructuring  Contribute towards influencing the GSDR (and the G20 beyond it) and the World Bank and IMF’s Debt Sustainability Framework review to promote debtor countries’ interests.  Conduct country-specific independent research reports (Malawi and Zambia) on debt sustainability and promote a series of country-specific workshops on debt sustainability and debt restructuring
3.4.2.2 Tax systems are fair within SAF
 Undertake one feasibility study of wealth tax inin Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Malawi  Work with national, regional and global alliances to influence the new proposed UN global tax system.  Connecting national and regional (TJNA, SAPSN, CIVICUS and other CSO networks) taxation initiatives to global movements on fair tax systems such as the World Economic Forum and the 2024 Davos Week of Action  Secure spaces in print and electronic(Radio, TV, etc.) media clubs in Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Malawi for fair and just taxation and budget practices to influence further public and political debate.  Analysis on progressivity and gender sensitivity of tax policies in Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Malawi  Strengthen the capacity of Government fiscal officers in Double Taxation regime to improve legal framework for domestic resource mobilisation in Mozambique
3.4.2.3. Progressive spending on essential services such as health, education, and social protection
 Based on the CRI report work and together with regional partners to engage the SADC PF and the ECOSSOCC secretariatand provide advisory submissions to support their work in monitoring of member states’ performance on the CRI  Make pre-national budget submissions and undertake post national budget analysis and provide recommendations, extension of the work in Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Malawi  Undertake budget tracking on public resource allocation and utilization in health, education and social protection in Zambia, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and Malawi  Undertake research to strengthen the evidence base on public revenue collection and public spending  Lobby to influence decision makers on public revenue collection, public spending and progressive policies onpublic services spending Strategic Objective 3.4.3: Trade and Food Systems in SAF are Fair and Sustainable.
3.4.3.1 Increase by 20% the number of men and women smallholder farmers in vulnerable areas reached with interventions that aim to enhance inclusivity, productivity, and sustainability of food systems (Production).
 Support capacity building in Climate Smart Agriculture  Support capacity building of smallholder farmers to access finance and agricultural inputs/technologies.  Promote Digitally enabled solutions in agriculture, including integration of cashless transactions in agriculture value chains to improve efficiency and convenience. Advocacy on increased budget allocation towards agriculture and nutrition sector (Malawi) 3.4.3.2 Increase by 20% the number of womensmallholder farmers in targeted vulnerable areas who progressively trade in commercialised agro-food value chains and realize a living income from agriculture (Commercialisation and trade)  Support training in financial literacy and farming as a business among smallholder farmers.  Capacity development for youth-led and women-led agribusiness SMEs to provide servicesthat enhance commercialisation of smallholder agriculture.  Promote Market linkages for women smallholder farmers.  Facilitate development of cooperatives  Advocacy on decentralization of cooperative development policy (Malawi)  Promote inclusiveand responsible large-scale land-based investments (Malawi) and scale up the learning to other SAF cluster countries
3.4.3.3 Knowledge and innovation systems
 Increase by 10% the number of smallholder farmers applying new technologies/digital solutions/agricultural practices that aim to transformthe food systems towards increased productivity, income, and resilience.
3.4.3.4 Policy Environment
 Support capacity building of relevant national institutions to domesticate major international/national policy frameworks that advance food system transformation towards desirable outcomes (CAADP, ….)  Support Policy analysis on fairness in at least two selected commercialised agro-food value chains  Identify and engage regional and national Food system transformation think-tanks to convene at least 2 food system transform policy dialogues at national/regional levels.  Produce and disseminate at least 2 Policy briefs on fair trade and food system transformation.  Support Policy Advocacy for food system transformation and CAADP implementation.
Climate Justice in SAF
Strategic Objective 3.4.4: Greenhouse gas emissions are reduced to limit global heating by 1.5 degrees Celsius.
3.4.4.1 Produce and disseminate one Climate Justice trends report focusing on implementation of Nationally Determined Contributions in SAF countries.
3.4.4.2 Working with national/regional think-tanks Convene national/regional policy dialogues on Just Energy Transition and Just Agro-food system transformation.
3.4.4.3 Contribute towards Oxfam wide global GHGe reduction agenda.
 Increased involvement by women and youth in eco-friendly economic enterprises in Zomba and Chokwe Districts  Promote equitable access to clean energy including for cookingand heating by households (Malawi). This includes engagement with IFIs to prioritize investment in clean energy sectors
Strategic Objective 4.4.5. Local expertise and women’s leadership is resourced to build resilience and shape solutions. 4.4.5.1 Empower communities and amplify the voices of livid experiences to challenge climate change narratives.
 Create opportunities to learn fromthe experiences of people affected by climate change.  Co-develop consistent, coordinated, and culturally appropriate communication resources that reflect everyday experiences of climate change.  Hold community forums and engagement activities on localised issues of climate justice.
4.4.5.2 10% of the poor and marginalised women covered by Oxfam SAF programmes have been adequately resourced to have a voice to build and shape locally led adaptation and resilience solutions in targeted vulnerable areas.
4.4.5.3 Capacitydevelopment: Leverage the diverse work within the Oxfam confederation to promote capacity strengthening and knowledge sharing on resilience building using locally led solutions.
 Increased participation, leadership and influence of women in community-level, national and international climate change negotiations Strategic Objective 3.4.6. Climate finance is adequate, predictable, and accessible for the poor and vulnerable communities. 3.4.6.1 Increase by 50% the amount of climate adaptation finance accessed by the pillar and supporting poor and vulnerable communities in targeted vulnerable areas.  Support partners to access climate finance and implement locally led climate action  Support CBOs and the African Group of Negotiators to engage with national and global climate processes such as UNFCCC’s COP processes (including the COP28)  Undertake researc to generate knowledge/evidence to support Oxfam Climate Justice campaign on: (a) cost of climate damage/loss and adaptation cost; (b) climate finance flows to SAF (Malawi, Mozambique, Zambia, Zimbabwe) and actual spent in vulnerable communities; c) adaptation costs  In collaboration with the Comms team and Humanitarian team develop responsive, broad-based, informative, and mixed media communications products on the impact of climate change on frontline communities in Zimbabwe, Zambia and Mozambique  Advocate for increased climate finance to support locally led adaptation and resilience initiatives
3.4.6.2 Influencing:
 Facilitate, support, and coordinate a series of climate conversations (twice a year on any of the following priority themes: Just Transition, Climate Finance, Locally Led Adaptation, Climate Change and Gender, Goal on Adaptation; Ecosystem Based Adaptation, Climate  Action on Agriculture and Food Security, Loss and Damage, Climate Change and Human Settlement planning, etc) at national and regional level that influence climate policy at national, regional and global levels.
Accountable Governance:
Strategic Objective 3.4.7: Robust governance frameworks provide safe spaces for people to hold duty bearers to account.
 Increase by 20% the number of civil society, communities, and government extractive governance engagements suchas the Mining Indabas, law reform efforts.  Support advocacy for the repeal of legislation shrinking civic space and accountable governance in Zimbabwe, Mozambique, and Zambia  Support advocacy for increased disclosure of mining, oil and gas contracts/licenses,revenue collected and environmental and social information by governments in SAF.

participating-org.narrative: Oxfam Novib is one of the 17 national affiliates of the Oxfam International Confederation. It started life in 1956 as the Netherlands Organisation for International Assistance (Novib), and joined forces with Oxfam in 1994. Working together in confederation, the Oxfam affiliates can speak with one clear and compelling voice on issues of global concern: climate change, health and education forall, agriculture, trade, and conflicts and emergencies. Oxfam established this country office to support local organizations and projects. Through this local office Oxfam Novib directly contributes towards this project’s implementation.
